fields.title: A build of kac takes whichever .NET 10 SDK the runner installs

sections.What we are doing instead:
Each job that builds it installs the SDK with [tol-setup-dotnet] and `dotnet-version: 10.0.x`, which takes the newest 10.0 SDK on the day. [tol-dotnet-sdk] approves the same range. No `global.json` fixes the version, so version control alone does not say which SDK built a commit.

The package published to nuget.org is built once, by the publish workflow, from the commit on `main`. Its run log shows the SDK that job installed.
sections.Why we need it: Fixing the version needs a `global.json` and a way to move it when a patch ships, and neither has been set up. The range takes each SDK patch without a pull request.
sections.What the risk is: Two builds of one commit run on different SDK patches, and a difference between them shows only in the package that shipped. Nothing here would explain it without reading both run logs. An SDK patch seldom changes what a build produces, so the cost is a confusing difference and not a broken release.
sections.What compensates:
* The publish workflow is the only thing that builds what ships, and its run log records the commit and the SDK.
* [ctl-0007] packs the tool and installs it on every pull request. That copy runs `kac new` and validates the corpus
  it created, so a build that cannot run is caught before it ships.
* nuget.org never lets a published version be replaced, so a rebuild cannot overwrite what people already have.
sections.How it closes: A `global.json` names the exact SDK, every workflow installs the version it names, and something moves it when a patch ships. This record closes when that file is in the repository. [#971](https://github.com/paul80nd/knowledge-as-code/issues/971) tracks the work.
sections.Scope: Every build of `kac`: the publish workflow, CI, and a contributor's own machine.
